prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
(empty)

New part:
U0001: 1.
U0002: Introduction In the present day National Airspace System (NAS), the air traffic management (ATM) system has a predicted trajectory for each flight based on the approved flight plan and a scheduled or controlled departure time.
U0003: Once the aircraft starts to move, controllers tactically manage the aircraft, using “open trajectory” vectors, altitude changes, and speed clearances, to implement traffic management restrictions, separate otherwise conflicting aircraft, and address arising NAS constraints.
U0004: The current ATM system tends to be conservative in the strategic time frame, when changes are implemented via flight plan changes, to avoid delaying aircraft more than necessary.
U0005: As a result, many problems are left to the controller to solve tactically (e.g., routing an aircraft around weather or complying with a new Traffic Flow Management [TFM] restriction).
U0006: Tactical controller actions are not directly communicated to the automation systems or other stakeholders.
U0007: These aspects of the current system, coupled with gaps in trajectory prediction data and models, impede the ability to predict how NAS constraints will influence a flight’s trajectory.
U0008: Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) assign departure times designed to comply with a Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA) at a NAS constraint, based on the airspace user’s estimated time en route but without knowledge of controller actions to address other constraints.
U0009: Time Based Flow Management (TBFM) makes a similar assumption that the estimated times of arrival (ETAs) to the constraint are correct, when a variety of disruptions can introduce unexpected delays that affect the flight’s ETA.
U0010: Until the flight is affected, the impact of local traffic management decisions on individual flights is not known, and a flight may encounter several such disruptions en route to its destination.
U0011: This makes NAS demand predictions at each NAS resource less accurate.
U0012: Management by Trajectory (MBT) is a concept for future ATM in which the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and airspace users negotiate four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs) for all flights that respect the airspace user’s goals while complying with NAS constraints.1 By considering both airspace user and FAA objectives, and utilizing negotiated 4DTs to communicate the traffic management plan, the concept is highly flexible to different types of airspace users and trajectory characteristics.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
response:
{"summary":"Context: National Airspace System (NAS); air traffic management (ATM) system; actors: controllers, airspace users, Federal Aviation Administration (FAA); stakeholders and automation systems receive no direct communication of current tactical controller actions.
Current ATM: The ATM system predicts each flight’s trajectory from its approved flight plan and scheduled or controlled departure time. Strategic management implements changes through flight plan changes and is conservative to avoid unnecessary delays. Once an aircraft moves, controllers tactically manage it using “open trajectory” vectors, altitude changes, and speed clearances to implement traffic management restrictions, separate conflicting aircraft, and address NAS constraints. Tactical problems include weather avoidance and compliance with new Traffic Flow Management (TFM) restrictions. Uncommunicated controller actions and gaps in trajectory prediction data/models impede prediction of constraint effects.
Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) assign departure times intended to satisfy a Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA) at a NAS constraint. They use the airspace user’s estimated time en route without knowledge of controller actions addressing other constraints. Time Based Flow Management (TBFM) similarly assumes estimated times of arrival (ETAs) at constraints are correct. Disruptions and local traffic management decisions can cause unexpected delays; effects on individual flights remain unknown until experienced, and multiple disruptions reduce demand-prediction accuracy at NAS resources.
Future concept: Management by Trajectory (MBT) is future ATM in which FAA and airspace users negotiate four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs) for all flights. Negotiated 4DTs communicate the traffic management plan. Trajectories must respect airspace user goals while complying with NAS constraints; the concept considers both FAA and airspace user objectives and accommodates different airspace user types and trajectory characteristics."}
